item.title: The Music Room, behind the yurt, for anybody who only wants to listen
item.description: A door beside the phonograph in the Faery Yurt opens the Music Room, at Helen’s ask, for those who just want to listen and not scroll: the phonograph with her whole playlist on it and every song on the yarn as a record in an arched case, in a room with nothing else in it. The yurt keeps its own phonograph; the music is in both rooms, written into each by the one tool from the one data file, so they cannot say different things. Join the faeries and Grow a garden are in there too. It is the Reading Room’s house one door along, the gothic dark academia she asked for: claret walls, a chandelier, candles in brass sconces that never flicker, ravens, a pointed window open on the night with a moon and a bare branch behind it, a cello and a harp that make no sound, and a cobweb in the corner. The record turns at MAX and nowhere else, as it does in the yurt. A job marker of its own, a moth asleep on the phonograph’s horn, on the guild’s board; a card, a place on the map, a line on Now Playing and a fractal window, like every room.

item.title: Every spine in the yurt’s bookcases opens its author’s Wikipedia page
item.description: The seven cases that were lettered plain now open like the Art shelf, at Helen’s ask, which was her first that day: every author on Poetry, Novels, Philosophy, Old Classics, Earth & Kin, Myth & Otherworlds and Liberation & Rest is a door to their page on English Wikipedia, wrapped the way the Art shelf’s spines already were, in the spine’s own cream with only the underline saying link. The order and the colours of the spines are unchanged. Every address was checked on the day, each one answering 200 from Wikipedia without a redirect, and the pen names, mononyms and shared names were read before they were linked: Spinoza, Chaucer and Shakespeare to the people and not the disambiguation pages; bell hooks to the author; Nick Walker to the scholar of the neurodiversity paradigm; David Mitchell and Joyce Johnson to the novelists; Mark Fisher and Erin Manning to the theorists; and Lewis Carroll to the author, not the book. Four names that Wikipedia keeps under another title (Anna Tsing, Mark Fisher, Erin Manning, adrienne maree brown) link to the page itself rather than through a redirect. One spine stays plain: Astrida Neimanis has no article on English Wikipedia, so her spine is lettered and opens nothing, rather than opening the wrong page or a search.

item.title: The yurt’s bookshelf becomes eight arched bookcases, with an art gallery under them
item.description: Seventy-two books now, up from twelve, at Helen’s ask: Kimmerer, Manning, Bergson, Nick Walker, adrienne maree brown, Ahmed, Braidotti, Barad, Hersey, Tsing, Sheldrake, Mary Oliver, bell hooks, Audre Lorde, Le Guin, the Brontës, Shakespeare, Frazer’s Golden Bough and many more, with Robert Graves on the myth shelf for The White Goddess. Deleuze and Guattari have a spine each, and Alice in Wonderland is shelved under Lewis Carroll, so every spine names an author. The one long shelf is now eight narrow arched bookcases, one for each kind of book: Poetry, Novels, Philosophy, Old Classics, Earth & Kin, Myth & Otherworlds, Liberation & Rest, and Art. Inside each, the books go alphabetically by surname. Cases standing side by side are the same height, so a shorter one has empty shelves waiting for what comes back from being lent out. An art gallery under the bookcases, at Helen’s ask: eleven paintings she keeps going back to, Pre-Raphaelites, Watts’s Hope and two Malevich squares, each out of copyright everywhere and each a scan Wikimedia Commons carries a public domain statement for, hung small on the wall and pressed off it into a gilt frame drawn in her room’s own colours. Every one is credited in the liner notes, with the painter, title and year read off the scan’s own record. The artists she named whose work is still their own — Goldsworthy, Rothko, Hepworth, Pollock, Flavin, Judd, Fontana, Knoebel, Morellet, Reinhardt — are spines on the Art shelf that open their Wikipedia pages, and nothing of theirs is shown. The caption under the staircase now reads, in her words, that some nights the library turns into a masquerade ballroom, and asks whether you want to join her.

item.title: The guest bar’s teleporter goes where you pick again
item.description: Picking a room in the teleporter on the guest bar did nothing, whether you clicked it or pressed Enter, ever since the bar learned to sign you on. The Sign on button and the teleporter’s way of going somewhere had the same name in guest.js, and the button won. It has a name of its own now, and both work. The radio’s teleporter, for anybody signed on, was never affected.

item.title: Every room in the Faery Yurt has its own address
item.description: Each part of the yurt can be linked to now, at Helen’s ask, so the doorways on her Autistic Realms and More Realms About pages open straight onto it: #soundtrack, #bookshelf, #glimmer-window, #regulation-nook, #nature-notes, #who-lives-here, #pebbles and #where-to-find-me. Nothing on the page looks any different.

item.title: The yurt’s faeries come in three sizes and never fly over the words
item.description: Three sizes of faery, at Helen’s ask: little ones, ones three times as big, and the biggest four times as big. No faery ever flies over a word or a picture, at her ask. They live on the page now rather than on the window, so the words never slide under them as you scroll; each one only goes where there is room for all of it, and flies round the words from one open space to the next, so the big ones keep to the margins and the little ones slip through the gaps between the sections. A petal or a star that drifts onto a word is gone at once.

item.title: Bright red and rainbow hair at the Bodymind Booth
item.description: Two new hair colours, at Helen’s ask: bright red, and rainbow, which runs red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet from the roots down, on every hairstyle, long or short. A bodymind wearing either walks into the Dopamine Dress-Up Den with it, and keeps it as a CB avatar.

item.title: Woodland faeries in the yurt, and a new portrait by the door
item.description: The faeries are small woodland faeries now, at Helen’s ask: each a tiny figure with a flower crown, long hair, a mossy cloak to the ground, a posy held in front and gauzy wings, and some with little curled horns. Their skin, hair and cloaks vary so no two are dressed alike. They are drawn here, not taken from anybody’s artwork. They float more slowly, and each lets fall petals that drift down, sway and fade over three seconds; nothing blinks. At MAX GLITTER they still glow brighter and leave stars. A new portrait of Helen beside the welcome, sent by her today: Helen in a sunlit wood. Her description of the old one still fits it, so it carries those words until she changes them. The earlier photograph stays on Enid’s wall. Not cropped, not filtered, and re-saved with no metadata.

item.title: The yurt’s garden grows round the words, and the faeries come in colours and leave stars
item.description: Grow a garden grows on the page now, at Helen’s ask: tangled ivy along the top of the page and along the foot, strands hanging down and climbing up, ivy down the margins either side, small flowers in every colour (yellows, blues, reds, pinks, lilacs, oranges and creams), red and brown toadstools growing in the ivy, and mushrooms coming up out of the bottom. It grows along the green sprigs too, and across the open space between the sections. Most of it has grown in about twenty seconds, and then for about two minutes more it keeps slowly adding more ivy, leaves, flowers and mushrooms. It never covers a word or a picture: it measures where they are and grows round them, and if the page changes shape it grows round the new shape. The faeries are all different, at her ask: every one a different size and a different muted colour, dusty rose, sage, lavender, slate blue, old gold, mauve. At MAX GLITTER they are much brighter and leave a trail of stars, each fading out over a second and a half, so nothing blinks or flashes. The nook’s coffee is coffee and tea: the tile reads a standing supply of coffee and tea, and Ryan’s “Ahhhh.” is still behind it.

item.title: The Live Room gets the glass, and the studios’ own month under the desk
item.description: The Live Room’s desk is a rack now. Every strip still plays where it hangs, and a second button puts it up on the glass over the desk instead, saying how long it runs before you press it. Taking it off puts the glass back as it was and plays nothing, and each studio’s desk folds away. Under the desk, the last month off each studio’s own channel: Austin City Limits, KEXP and KCRW, their videos and their shorts, newest first, refilled every morning. Nobody chose these or watched them first, so there is no tape on them. Nobody has checked where each was played either: the rule that a session was played indoors is still the desk’s, and the room says so beside the month. KEXP puts up each session whole and then every song from it on its own, more in three days than YouTube’s feed for a channel carries. So the new puller reads a channel’s own list page, past its first hundred, whenever the feed does not reach back to what an earlier morning covered, rather than printing a gap for a month while the mornings fill it in. It met YouTube’s new shape for an upload list’s rows the same night, and reads both.

item.title: Plath in the Zibaldone, as she printed it
item.description: Sylvia Plath’s line from The Bell Jar is in the Zibaldone, sent in by Betsy and read by Ryan in a reissue made from Faber and Faber’s 1966 edition. It came in joined by a colon. In the book the sentence ends at heart, and I am, I am, I am stands as a paragraph of its own, so the leaf sets them on two lines. The reissue is public domain in Canada and not everywhere, and Plath is still in copyright under the room’s test, so the line is quoted short and cited, and the leaf links the Faber edition rather than the reissue.

item.title: Your Room says what to do, how to send it, and what happens next
item.description: People told us they read Your Room and did not know what they were supposed to do next. It says so near the top now: build it with us or build it with your AI, then send it to us. How to ask is Build it with us, and it lists the questions to answer: the same questions the prompt has your AI ask you. They are read out of the prompt every time the street is built, so the two can never ask different things. How to submit your room says where to send it whichever way you made it, what to send, and what to leave in. What happens next says what we do with it, how soon we write back, what decides how long the rest takes, and how to change the room later. The line comparing you to Enid is gone. It only made sense if you already knew who Enid is. Changed: your-room.html, data/community.json and the service board in community-center.html, a new tools/make-your-room.py in tools/check-all.sh, README.md.

item.title: Patches for your battle jacket
item.description: Patches lie about the street now, and some are on a counter in a shop, free to take. Signed on to the CB, pick one up and it is sewn on your battle jacket, a denim jacket in Profile on the radio. Every patch is its own size, shape and design, drawn in its own room’s colours and lettered in its own room’s typeface, and all of them sew onto the same jacket. The first ones: Stimpunks.World on the pavement, Pink Pony Peep on the dancefloor, Interdependence in the Town Hall, Kindness Is Punk on Club Chronic’s distro table, Plant-Powered on Vital Plant Living’s counter, Intermittently Social Lone Wolf in the Cave, and Synapse of the Soil at the end of Mycelium Munchies’ pass. Where the patches are, under your jacket in Profile, lists them all. Show my battle jacket on the CB, with a claimed username, shows it in your profile, and Sticker on the radio sends a patch to the channel. The street keeps which patches are on your jacket and nothing about when, nothing counts who else has one, and Forget me takes them all off.

item.title: Rescue Ranger and Pet Parent, the Guild’s first badges that are not jobs
item.description: Rescue Ranger is for anybody who rescues an animal at one of the shelters, and Pet Parent for anybody who adopts one. Like every badge, each is worked out from what you have already done, and kept nowhere. Rescue Ranger is only ever yours to see. The shelters promise that nothing on the street knows who rescued which animal, and the only list of the animals you rescued is in your own browser. So the badge is shown on the Guild’s board and in your own Profile, and never on your profile for anybody else. Pet Parent comes from the pets in your Profile, so the board shows it while you are signed on to the CB, and other people see it in your profile only if you show your pets.

item.title: The Guild’s board filters, keeps your jobs in your Profile, and gives out badges
item.description: The jobs can be filtered: every job, the ones you have not handed in, or the ones you have. The filter hides rows and never says how many. Signed on to the CB, the board can keep your jobs in your Profile. Keep my jobs in my Profile, beside the hand-in box, starts off. Switched on, it keeps the jobs this browser has stamped and every one you hand in after, so they follow you to any device you sign on with. It keeps which jobs, and nothing about when. Profile on the radio lists them, and with a claimed username Show my jobs on the CB shows them in your profile, the way pets and avatars are shown. Switching keeping off deletes them, and so do Forget me and deleting your username. Privacy has it all. Badges, because people asked, after merit badges, Open Badges and video game achievements. A badge is a set of jobs that go together: the rooms down the lift, the tables on the street, the toys. It is worked out from the jobs you have handed in every time, and kept nowhere. Nothing counts them, none is rare or secret, none ever asks for more than it did when it was posted, and none certifies anything. Each one has its own drawing, stamped in the guild’s vermilion when it is yours. This reverses part of one of the board’s own rules, on Ryan’s call. The tool that builds the board used to refuse the word badge on it. It still refuses it in a job’s own words, and it refuses a badge that is ranked, rare, unlocked, counted or certifies anything. No badge sends anybody to a room for resting in, because on this street rest is owed rather than earned, and a badge is earned.

item.title: The Faery Yurt: a field book, a picnic hamper, a turret window, faeries and a garden
item.description: Nature Notes is an old field book now, at Helen’s ask. Shut, it is bound in leather with its name in gold; press it and it opens onto ruled cream pages, each photograph mounted whole with photo corners and a note under it in her hand. The notes are Helen’s own words from the line above the book, on the pictures they fit; the other pages are ruled and waiting. Close the book shuts it again, and with scripts off the book is simply open. The basket by the door is a picnic hamper, at Helen’s ask: pale woven willow, a gingham lining in her ivy, the lid propped open behind, and leather straps and brass buckles down the front. The pebbles sit in the lining, and nothing about taking one has changed. Join the faeries, and grow a garden, two switches under the dial, at Helen’s ask. One sends a few small faeries drifting across the page; the other grows ivy down both edges of the window and toadstools in the bottom corners, very slowly. Each stays still until somebody presses it, at every setting, and pressing again clears it. Nothing flashes and nothing is remembered. The dial’s small print in the yurt now says nothing else moves unless you ask it to, where it used to say nothing else ever moves. The glimmer window is a castle turret’s window, at Helen’s ask: a round arch in stone, and shutters of oak planks with iron strap hinges and studs that close into one arched door. Her photographs open behind them as before, each kept clear of the arch so none is cut.

item.title: Beauvoir in the Zibaldone, read in the book
item.description: The first line in the Zibaldone to come in by the new way is Simone de Beauvoir’s, from The Second Sex, sent in by Betsy. Ryan read it on page 273 of H. M. Parshley’s English, published by Jonathan Cape, where it opens the chapter called Childhood, and it came in exactly as printed. The leaf names Parshley as well as Beauvoir, because a translation is somebody’s work too, and it says the title page gives no year.

item.title: The Zibaldone takes its first lines from somebody else’s hand
item.description: Betsy sent lines in for the Zibaldone, and two are in the book, with her name on their citations: Louisa May Alcott’s storms, from Little Women, and a sentence of Whitman’s from Song of Myself. Both were read in the printings their cards name. Alcott wrote I’m where it came in as I am, and the line is Amy’s. Whitman’s line ends in a comma and the sentence goes on for two more lines, so the leaf carries all three. This changes one of the room’s rules, on Ryan’s call. Until today a line still in copyright could only come in if one of our own pages already quoted it, which meant the room could never take one from anybody who sent it. Now it can also come in once a person has read it in the book itself, and its card says who read it and on which page. The checking did not get any looser: a line copied off a quotation site still counts as unread, and tools/make-zibaldone.py refuses a line with no record of who read it, or where. The rest of what Betsy sent is waiting to be read in the book, and nothing goes on the page until somebody has. One of those lines is usually credited to a different writer from the one it came in under, which is exactly what reading it in the book is for.

item.title: Avatars in profiles, large, and in the lightbox
item.description: A profile on the CB shows the avatar its person wears, first and large enough to see its details, when you press their name on Who’s online or their handle on the channel. Press it to open it in the lightbox, as large as the window allows. The rest of somebody’s avatars show only if they say so. Show my avatars on the CB, in Profile, is off until you switch it on and needs a claimed username, the same as showing your pets. The privacy page says what it keeps.

item.title: The Faery Yurt’s residents open onto their photographs
item.description: Every card under Who Else Lives Here in the Faery Yurt opens now, at Helen Edgar’s ask: the cats onto Cats Coven, every photograph of Harry, Zara, Ziggy and Tiggy together; Benji onto the Dog’s Den; and Gibbles onto the Hamster Haven. Press a card to open it and again to shut it; nothing loads until it is open.

item.title: Nature Notes is a notebook now
item.description: In the Faery Yurt, Helen’s Nature Notes became a notebook, at her ask: a bound cover in the yurt’s wood, cream pages, and one photograph to a page, shown whole. Swipe the pages, or press Turn the page and Turn back; a screen reader hears each photograph’s description as its page turns. A shadow sweeps across the page as it turns, only when you press, and not at all at Gentle, where the page simply changes. The notebook stores nothing and never turns a page by itself.

item.title: The Bodymind Booth, and avatars on the CB
item.description: The Bodymind Booth is open, next door to the Dopamine Dress-Up Den: a photo booth with no camera in it, where you draw your bodymind. How you get about, on your feet, in a wheelchair or in a power chair; your height, shoulders, middle and hips; your skin, numbered rather than named, with four colours nobody is born in; your face and your hair; and everything you always have with you, from glasses, hearing aids, cochlear implants, ear defenders and masks to canes, crutches, walkers, AAC devices, fidgets, chew necklaces and prosthetics. No body comes first: the booth opens on somebody drawn at random. The idea came from our community, from somebody who hoped for characters to dress one day. Take it next door and dress it. The Dress-Up Den now asks who is wearing it, the stand or your bodymind, and every garment on its rails is drawn again to fit whoever puts it on, standing or sitting. Avatars, kept in Profile on the CB. Keep a bodymind, or an outfit on the stand, as an avatar; with a claimed username, wear one at a time beside your name on Who’s online and change which whenever you like; and send any of them as a sticker. A screen reader hears an avatar as what its owner wrote about it and nothing else. Two things written down here before have changed, both Ryan’s calls. The Dress-Up Den had recorded any drawing of a body as not open; the Den still draws none of its own, and the bodies are drawn in a booth of their own, where nobody is handed one. And pets were the one thing the street kept under a person; avatars are the second, deleted by Forget me and by deleting your username, and never a picture: an avatar is a list of choices.

item.title: The Faery Yurt’s residents have names, and Helen’s photographs are up
item.description: The residents of the Faery Yurt are named now: the cats are Harry, Zara, Ziggy and Tiggy, the dog is Benji and the hamster is Gibbles. Cats Coven is a gallery of the four cats together, and Nature Notes, in the regulation nook, is Helen Edgar’s own photographs from outdoors: flowers in her hair, boots by a stream, conkers on moss, an autumn tree and a good many mushrooms. Every one is hers, recorded like every photograph on the street, shown at its own shape and not filtered. No mushroom is named, on purpose. A photograph of a corner of Helen’s own room hangs in the regulation nook too. The glimmer window looks out onto Helen’s photographs now. Open the shutters and they are there, a strip of her own pictures of the woods, the snow, the bluebells, her room and her animals, each shown whole. Swipe or scroll through them, or use the buttons; at MAX GLITTER they roll on by themselves and can be paused, and they never move while the shutters are shut. Where To Find Me links her writing on Autistic Realms and More Realms, in her own words about each.

item.title: The Faery Yurt’s welcome, rewritten by Helen
item.description: Helen Edgar rewrote the welcome in her yurt, bringing in her own words from More Realms: the way in by the fairy lights from the treeline, the door flap that is always open, and a realm that is not a place of conclusions or answers but of threads, glimmers and soft, weird spaces. The yurt now says Stimpunks.World where it said Stimpunks Love.

item.title: A phonograph in the Faery Yurt, and every song on Helen’s yarn on a rack
item.description: The Faery Yurt has a phonograph, at Helen Edgar’s ask: a brass horn with pressed petals, a carved case, turned columns and a crank, drawn after a photograph she sent and only in colours her room already had. It takes the place of the little record beside her soundtrack, and like that record it turns at MAX GLITTER and nowhere else. Every song on her yarn is on a rack under it, also her ask. Each one says how long it runs before you press it, and plays where it hangs or goes up on the phonograph in place of the whole yarn; taking it off puts the yarn back without starting it. AURORA’s Echo of My Shadow plays again, on the rack. The copy on the playlist stopped playing, YouTube saying only that the video is unavailable, so its card plays the visualiser on AURORA’s own channel, the same song at the same length, and says so. The playlist is Helen’s, and the whole yarn reaches the old copy until she swaps it.

item.title: The Sandbox, its suggestion box, and building the street with us
item.description: The Sandbox is open, a shopfront on the street: a room thought up by somebody in our community and built with Claude, an AI made by Anthropic, and brought onto the street from the page they made. A laptop left open in the sand at dusk, its screen the only light in the playground: come in curious, try things, break things and tell us what you notice, with no deadlines and nothing to lose. There is a sandcastle you can build and burn down, and the ball bounces. Its credit is in the liner notes, with the other rooms people built, and Rubik Dirt, by NaN and Luke Prowse, is a new face on the street, for the sign on its box. Its suggestion box works. Anybody signed on to the CB can drop in a suggestion, a feature request or a bug report, about the room or anywhere on the street, with their handle on it. Anybody can read what is in the box, and our moderators answer each one, done or not doing, always with a reply and their own username on it. It stays until whoever dropped it in or a moderator takes it down, and nothing in it is counted, ranked or voted on. Privacy says what the box keeps, and the community service board has a slot for it. And you can build the street with us. Under the box are the steps: make your own copy of the code, check your computer with tools/setup.sh, hook up Claude, see the street on your own computer, make a change, check everything, and send it back as a pull request. The same steps are CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository, written from the same place so the two cannot disagree. We made two small changes to the room’s page, so the street has somewhere to put its box and its steps: a space round its own link to us, which is still there with scripts off, and a space after its box. Everything else in the room is its maker’s, as they made it.

item.title: A call that follows you: Pop out
item.description: Pop out, on a call’s window, moves the call into a browser window of its own, which stays open while you go from room to room in the window you came from. It works for the World call and for any room’s call, signed on to the CB. You join again in the new window, because a call cannot be carried from one window to another without starting over. The radio knows where the call is on every page: the call’s own button stays pressed, Show the call window brings the window to the front, and pressing the call’s button again hangs up and closes it. There is still one call at a time. The CB guide has it, and Privacy says what the window sends and keeps, which is nothing new.

item.title: The World call
item.description: A call for the whole street: Join World call, under Who’s around on the radio, opens one call that is no room’s, from any page, for anybody signed on to the CB. It opens in the same window as a room’s call, and you are in one call at a time. The CB guide has it. Like every call, it hangs up when you leave the page, and going to another room is leaving the page, because every room is a page of its own. The radio says so when it opens. Who’s online names it in Calls going now while somebody is in it, and nobody is shown who is in it before they join. Privacy says so.

item.title: The CB in parts, where you are, and calls on Who’s online
item.description: The radio is in parts now, each under a heading: Where you are, Who’s around, Channel, Watching together and Your radio, with room and a groove in the case between them. This came out of people trying the CB: it had grown one button at a time into one long column, and it was hard to tell where one part ended. The headings are real ones, so a screen reader can move between them. Small is unchanged. The CB guide has the parts in order. The radio says which room you are in, at the top, in its largest words, because some people could not tell where they were. Tuned to World, you hear the whole street, and the radio now says where you are standing as well as what you are hearing. A name on Who’s online opens that person’s profile, the same as pressing their handle on the channel: their handle, its mark, and their pets if they show them. Who’s online lists the calls going now: every room whose call has somebody in it, with a link there. It names the room and nothing else, not who or how many. Who is in a call is still shown only in its room, to people seen there. Privacy says so, and a room the base keeps or one that keeps to itself is not named. Join this room’s call is under Where you are now, and Add my spot, Host this film and Screen a video are under Watching together, which is only there while one of them is.

item.title: More sticker sheets
item.description: The sticker drawer has more sheets: the days of the month, 1 to 31; the weeks of the year, 1 to 53; the words Week, Day, Month, Quarter and Year; this year’s number and next year’s, read off your own clock so they turn over on 1 January by themselves; the weather; and the moon. The weather and the moon are drawn here: cloudy, partly sunny, rainy, stormy, snowy, windy, sunny, a tornado and flooding, and the moon’s eight phases on round stickers, as they look from the northern hemisphere. Pictures are never turned on their side to fit more, because a sideways moon is a different phase. Every number is the same width, so a sheet of them reads as a grid, and a sheet of a set reads a set at a time: a moon sheet goes round the cycle, and a sheet of dates runs 1 to 31 and starts again. The first sheets went through the printer and cut cleanly, so the spacing stays as it is. One thing changed for sheets already printed: a word’s size is now worked out across every word, number and year the drawer can print, so a Monday and a 12 in one face match. In most faces nothing moved; in a few display faces a day or month comes out a little smaller than it did.

item.title: Sharing a sticker sheet
item.description: The sticker drawer can share a sheet now, wherever your browser can share a file. Share hands it to your device’s own share sheet, where Save Image puts it straight into a phone’s photos, which is where the Liene Photo app picks from. Save still puts it in your downloads. The site’s security headers were loosened by one word to do it: the share sheet was switched off for every page, and is now allowed to this site’s own pages, with the sticker drawer the only script that may open it. It sends nothing to us, and opens only when you press Share.

item.title: The Open Notebook’s sticker drawer
item.description: The Open Notebook has a sticker drawer: the days of the week and the months of the year, by name, on sheets for the PixCut S1, Liene’s photo sticker printer and cutter. Any typeface on the street, in three sizes, and the week or the year on one sheet, or a day or a month to a sheet. As many stickers to a sheet as will go. The week’s and the year’s sheets take as many whole weeks or years as fit, then whatever more will go in the gaps, turning some on their side where that fits more, and every sheet says underneath it what is on it. Where a whole year will not fit at Large, the sheet says which size it fits at. A sheet is a PNG the size of the paper at 300 dpi, clear everywhere but the stickers, so the Liene Photo app can cut round each one. It is drawn in your browser and saved to your own device, and carries the face’s designer and licence inside it. A rule of the room was narrowed for it. The Open Notebook refused any list to choose from and any script of its own, so that there would be nowhere to write. The drawer’s face picker is one list, and it has one script; neither takes a word, keeps anything or sends anything, and the room still has nowhere to write.

item.title: Wide-Spread Chaos Gardens
item.description: Wide-Spread Chaos Gardens is open, east of the stile in Nature’s Contribution: food and flowers from a mix of seed thrown into the wind, on a clear windy day with everything in the garden leaning the same way. The drawing is thrown too, out of a fixed seed, so it is the same garden every time. What chaos gardening is, and what it is not, in the words of a landscape specialist at Colorado State University Extension: a garden, not a restoration. The mix is half things to eat and half flowers, and the four noxious weeds Colorado State University Extension says to keep out of a seed mix are named and never in it. It gives food to the café in the old dairy and the honesty box, flowers and seed, and a bench in the middle with no paths to keep to. The screen in the seed shed has films about chaos gardens, meadows from seed and plants that sow themselves.

item.title: The Honesty Box
item.description: The Honesty Box is open on the street, a farm stand at the kerb lit by its own solar lamp, with the wool, hemp rope and cloth, pasteurised milk and cheese, eggs, meat and produce of the land past the campgrounds. Prices on the board, money in the box, and nobody watching. It is the one stall on the street with prices, because selling the land’s goods is the land’s half of the bargain with the street. Every item says what it costs and which place it came from, and the board is checked against what each place sends here. Never in the box: cannabis, which leaves the land through licensed dispensaries only, because a box nobody watches cannot ask anybody’s age; raw milk; and anything from the sanctuary.

item.title: The Dairy
item.description: The Dairy is open, behind All Together Now Farms: the farm’s old dairy is a café now, white glazed tile to the ceiling with the light going round and round it, and the pasteuriser still on the counter. Everything on the menu was grown on the land, and every dish says which places grew it, checked against each place’s own page; the salt and the baking soda are bought in, and it says so. Allergens are worked out from what is in each dish by Hey, Good Cookin’s engine, and each drink’s caffeine by Pekoe and Purrs’. Every milk and cheese is pasteurised.

item.title: All Together Now Farms
item.description: All Together Now Farms is open, north-east of the stile: a mixed farm where trees, crops and animals share the same fields, lit by the sun going down on one side and the full moon coming up on the other, so everything on it is warm on one side and silver on the other. The five agroforestry practices in the USDA’s own words, and which the farm does: four of them, and the fifth says why not. The Three Sisters are planted in the alleys between the nut trees and credited to the nations that teach them, with their story left to them. Sheep, goats and chickens, and the milk is pasteurised, with the CDC and Colorado’s law saying why. Everything the farm grows goes to the café in its old dairy and the honesty box on the street. The screen in the barn has films about growing, grazing and the Three Sisters, and the last month of Farming While Beige, refilled every morning.

item.title: Gentle Help Cannabis Farm
item.description: Gentle Help Cannabis Farm is open, north-west of the stile: cannabis in flower in hoop houses that glow through their own skin, grown among basil, dill, alfalfa, marigolds and the other plants a grower’s guide says grow well beside it. What each companion is supposed to do is said as the guide’s, beside an extension service saying research mostly does not back it. A table of strains, sativa, indica and hybrid, with Leafly’s lab-test figures for THC and CBD and the top terpenes. Leafly publishes no CBN, so the table says so. Under it, three papers saying the three words tell you little about what is in the jar, and that labels in Colorado read higher than the lab. Harm reduction, from our Addiction and Harm Reduction entries and from public health: edibles, driving, mixing, lungs, vapes, concentrates, synthetics, CHS, storage, and Colorado’s law, each with where it was read. Nothing is sold at the farm, nobody is called a name, and nothing on the page promises what cannabis will do for anybody. The screen in the potting shed has films about growing among companions, hemp to rope and cloth, and rosin.

item.title: Brighter Days Solar Farm
item.description: Brighter Days Solar Farm is open, north of the stile: panels on posts high enough to walk under, peppers, cherry tomatoes and basil in their shade, the farm’s sheep between the rows, and the power for the land and much of the street. It is built on Star Stuff’s Two Peppers and the field experiment behind it, quoted and credited: two peppers answered the same shade in two different ways, and neither is the failure case. The screen in the battery shed has films about crops, sheep and bees under solar panels, picked for the room and checked to play here.

item.title: All Needs Met
item.description: All Needs Met Wildlife Sanctuary is open, west of the stile in Nature’s Contribution: a wildlife preserve left to whatever was there first, and a home for good for animals who are disabled or were abandoned. You see it on the night round, through the viewer the keepers carry instead of a torch, so nobody is woken: every resident white with their own warmth, the night black, and nothing in the room with a colour, because heat has none. Eight residents, each with how they came, how they get about and what they like, and nobody called brave, sad or a lesson. They are this story’s animals, not real ones. The preserve’s wild neighbours have plain names, and nothing tells you how to find them. The screen in the keepers’ hut has a month of films from the fourteen channels Ryan listed, refilled every morning, the oldest going off the end. Nobody here watched them first, and every one says how long it runs before you press.

item.title: Nature’s Contribution
item.description: Past the campgrounds and through its wood, there is land now: Nature’s Contribution, kept for wildlife, for food and for power at once, where every part feeds the others and the street. It is built on a paper Ryan brought, “Balancing land use for conservation, agriculture, and renewable energy” (Nature Communications, 2026), and quotes it under its CC BY licence: some of the land is shared between uses and some is left to wildlife outright, because the paper is careful about what sharing ground can do. A fingerpost at the stile has an arm for every place: a wildlife sanctuary, a cannabis farm, a solar farm, a mixed farm with a café in its old dairy, and a chaos garden. The signs are up and the places open one by one; an arm with nothing behind it yet says so. A table says what each place gives and where it goes, most of it to the street through an honesty box. Cannabis leaves only through licensed dispensaries, never the honesty box, and nothing leaves the sanctuary but its manure. The light is an afternoon under broken cloud, and the shadows on the fields are the clouds’. You are standing in one at the stile. Nothing moves, at any setting. The wood stays unmapped: the campgrounds still says so, and now says where the track through it comes out. The map has the land past the wood, and the Adventurer’s Guild has a job out there, still class III.

item.title: Her records play here now
item.description: Every record in Words, Bud, Beats has a TIDAL player on its sleeve, which Kristina Brooke asked for when she sent the room. It is press-to-play like everything else here: nothing reaches TIDAL until you press, pressing brings in TIDAL’s own player, and the song starts when you press play there. The links to each song are still there, for anybody who would rather hear it somewhere else. Without a TIDAL account it plays a preview, and every button says so before you press it. The preview is not one length: a minute of one song and thirty seconds of two others, when we tried it, so no button puts a number on it. Each button gives the whole song’s length. TIDAL is on the privacy page with the other services a press can load, including that its player also loads Datadog, which TIDAL uses to watch how the player is working, in about one visit in ten. A room that comes in through Your Room can have TIDAL tracks as players now, and the prompt says how. The check that every video on the street still plays checks every TIDAL track too, and how long it runs.

item.title: Words, Bud, Beats
item.description: Words, Bud, Beats is Kristina Brooke’s room (she/her): an intimate salon at desert dusk, lit by one west window, with the plants and the knickknacks on the sill. Six records stand on her shelf, each pairing a few of her words with one song and one strain, and the Open mic corner has a slip for a pairing of your own, which you copy and keep; nothing on it is sent or saved. It is the second room to come in through Your Room. She designed it with Claude, following our prompt, and the words, the songs and the strains are hers. Every song is a link to Tidal, which opens off the street, so nothing in the room plays here. One line of hers was changed here, with Ryan’s say-so. The Copy button’s script spelled out the room’s address, and a room’s script on this street may not name an address, so it reads the address off the page instead. The slip still ends with the same address. The import tool learned three things from her room. A list in the notes that says - none means nothing, which is the prompt’s own shape. A colour property set on one of the room’s own rules counts as declared; the tool had been calling it unknown. And a room’s credit in the liner notes no longer says it was built with an AI twice, which NeuroHome’s did too. Ours: her share card, which carries her window lifted from the page, and her job on the Adventurer’s Guild board, with a carrot off the shopping list on her fifth record lying on her floor.

item.title: Take off your own message
item.description: Anybody on the CB can take their own message off the air now, asked for by Ryan. Take off, which only the base station had, is on every message you sent, beside Copy and React. It takes the message off for everybody, with its picture and reactions, and it cannot be put back. The base station still has it on every message, and clearing the whole channel is still the base’s alone. Yours means the handle on it, and two marks narrow that. A message marked CLAIMED comes off only for that username’s own password, so a name somebody else signs on as later cannot reach back to what was said under it, and one marked BASE only for the base. The server decides, every time; the radio only decides where to draw the button. A moderator can only take things off a channel they can hear. Taking a message off never asked whether a moderator was let into a private room at the Town Hall; it asks now, like everything else that touches a room’s channel. The keyboard is not dropped when a message goes. The button that had it goes with its message, so it moves to the message box instead of to nowhere. The privacy page, the house norms and the CB guide say so.

item.title: The start of the book, in her own voice
item.description: Swaying Sweetgrass has the start of the audiobook beside the book, found by Ryan: Google Play Books’ preview of Braiding Sweetgrass, read by Robin Wall Kimmerer herself, the preface and Planting Sweetgrass. It says how long it runs before you press it, and the borrow link for the rest is right under it. The check that every video on the street still plays now covers the fires on that room’s fire pit, which the Campfire at Cavendish Coworking reads too. They had been checked nowhere.

item.title: A screen on the wall of the watch room
item.description: The Events Room has a shared screen now, asked for by Ryan, with Schitt’s Creek on a rack under it: CBC’s ten scenes, Alexis and David’s timeline, the scenes the fans chose, and the rise of Rose Apothecary, in the order he gave them. Each says how long it runs before you press it, plays in its own card or goes up on the screen, and was checked on its own watch page first. It is the room’s first screen, so it is where the CB puts things. Somebody on the CB can host what is on theirs and others can follow, and a moderator’s Screen a video goes up on it, waiting for each follower’s own press. The screen is not lit. The lamp’s column is still the only light in the room and stays on the chart table, so the screen hangs on the whitewash and gives off nothing until somebody presses it. The room’s line that nothing in it moves now says nothing moves by itself, because the screen plays what somebody presses. A room behind a Cavendish door can carry a rack now, not only a Hang Suite, built from the same rules, and the check that every video on the street still plays reads the doors’ racks too.

item.title: More channels on the teaching screen
item.description: Hey, Good Cookin’’s rack has Munchies, Joshua Weissman and Strictly Dumpling on it now, added by Ryan. They come after the channels already there, in the order he gave them, and their videos and shorts are read with everybody else’s each morning. A channel added between fills says so rather than saying its feed came up short, because it has not been read yet.

item.title: A lift in the lighthouse
item.description: The Events Room had a ladder up to its call and no other way up. It says there is a lift now, from the Events door all the way up to the lantern, stopping at the watch room on the way, and that nobody asks which one you took. The heading over the call names the lift first, and the job on the Adventurer’s Guild’s board for that room says it takes the lift or the ladder. The lift is in the words and not yet in the drawing, which still shows the ladder going up into the light.

item.title: A second rack on the Green: the newest from the search
item.description: The Green’s screen under the porch roof has a second rack, under Ryan’s pick: the newest videos YouTube’s search finds about cities and towns making room for green. There is one search for each of Ryan’s topics: green spaces, green building, urban forests, urban farms, edibles, solarpunk and renewable energy. Anything on it can go up on the same screen. It is refilled every morning by a new script on the same timer as the other racks. The room says when it was last filled. Nothing older than a week stays on it. Nobody here chooses or watches these first, and the room says so. A video goes on only if its own title says what was searched for, it plays here, and its channel did not file it as a game or as music. That last rule is because most of what YouTube finds for solarpunk this week is people playing a video game called Solarpunk. There is one video from each channel and no title twice, and each search takes a turn, so no one search fills the rack. YouTube’s search no longer sorts by newest, so the rack asks for videos put up this week and works out which are newest from each video’s own page.

item.title: Calls can use your camera and microphone in Chrome
item.description: In Chrome, a room’s call could not switch on its camera, its microphone or a shared screen, and said you had refused them although nothing had ever asked you. That was this site’s fault, not 8x8’s and not yours: our security header gave those three to the call and deliberately not to our own pages, and a browser will only hand a frame what the page round it already has. So Chrome switched them off inside the call before it could ask. The header now gives them to our pages as well, so that the call can have them, and Chrome asks you the first time a call wants them. Because the call sits inside our page, Chrome’s question names stimpunks.world. This reverses the rule written down when calls arrived, that the page itself gets none of the three. That rule could not work. Our pages still never ask for any of the three themselves. The header used to keep that promise, and now the tool that writes the header does: it reads every script this site serves and refuses one that asks for a camera, a microphone or a screen. The privacy page’s sentence about it stays true, and Architecture now says how.

item.title: Who’s online, on the radio
item.description: A Who’s online button sits beside World and This room on the CB radio. It lists everybody who has switched on Be seen here, in alphabetical order, with the room each of them is in; a room’s name takes you there. Ryan asked for it because people want to know who is around and are having a hard time connecting. Anybody signed on can open it. This changes what Be seen here means. It used to show you only to people seen in the same room. Now it also puts your handle and your room on Who’s online for everybody on the CB. If you switched it on before today, it does more than it did when you pressed it, and switching it off takes you off the list at once. The privacy page says so. @ in Teleport finds people by part of their handle now, from the same list, and goes to their room. What you type after the @ stays in your browser. The Let people find me switch from earlier today is gone, because Who’s online does what it did. CLAIMED sits beside a claimed username on Who’s online and in the room’s seen line, the way it does on the channel, so somebody signed on under a name that is not theirs cannot pass for its owner. Names come in alphabetical order, nobody is counted, rooms kept for the people they are for are not named to anybody else, and nothing records who looked.

item.title: Find somebody by name with an @ in the teleporter
item.description: Type @ and somebody’s handle into the radio’s Teleport, press Enter, and it takes you to the room they are in. Helen Edgar asked for a way to find where people are, and Ryan suggested the teleporter. Nobody can be found until they choose to be. Be seen here only ever showed you to people in the same room, and that is what everybody who pressed it agreed to, so being found from anywhere is a second switch under it, Let people find me. It is off until you press it, your browser remembers it, and it only works while you are seen. Only a claimed username can be found, because an unclaimed handle is anybody’s who signs on with it, and somebody could sign on with your name and have people sent to them. Only somebody who can be found can look: the same one switch, both ways, that Be seen here and the Slake keep, and the street checks it, not only the radio. One whole handle, and never a list. Part of a handle finds nobody, and nothing offers names as you type, because a list of names to pick from would be a list of who is on. The answer is the room and nothing else; anybody who cannot be found, for any reason, is “nobody by that whole handle can be found right now”, and a room kept for the people it is for is never named to anybody else. Nothing records who looked for whom. The privacy page has a new section, Being found by name, and the CB guide and the Community Center describe the switch. The guest bar and the front page’s search say where an @ works.

item.title: Rolls on the player piano at A Quiet Pint
item.description: The pub’s player piano has a shelf of rolls now, at Ryan’s ask: rags and popular songs from the 1900s to the 1920s, and three rolls played for the Welte-Mignon reproducing piano. Two were played onto the paper by the composers themselves: Scott Joplin, in 1916, and Alexander Scriabin, in 1910. A roll plays as a strip of sound, not on a screen, so the pub still has no screen anywhere. It plays only when you press it, one roll at a time, and every roll says how long it runs before you press. Each is a recording of a real roll on Wikimedia Commons, public domain there, and nothing is fetched from Commons until you press. Nothing musical is hosted here. Every composer on the shelf died more than seventy years ago, so the music is free everywhere and not only in the United States. Several rolls were left off for that, and several files that turned out to be notation software playing sheet music rather than rolls. Every roll names its composers with their years, what roll it is, how the recording was made where its Commons page says so, and that page. Every runtime was measured off the file. The privacy page lists Wikimedia Commons among the services a press loads.

item.title: A Quiet Pint: a pub under the street, made like McAnally’s
item.description: A Quiet Pint is a new shopfront, at Ryan’s ask: a pub a few steps down from the street, made like McAnally’s in Jim Butcher’s Dresden Files. Thirteen tables, thirteen stools along a bar that meanders, thirteen carved columns, thirteen windows, thirteen mirrors and thirteen ceiling fans, as in the books, and no two of any of them alike. There is no television, no games machine and no jukebox, only a player piano. The only light is the street’s, through small windows at the level of the pavement, passed round the room by old mirrors, so it lands in patches, none the same shape, a little dimmer and a little green. Nobody lights a lamp and the stove is shut. Nothing in the pub moves, at any setting, the fans included. A table that fits you. The tables are all different heights, so the room has a plan of the floor and a list of every table in words, with boxes to tick for what you want: room under it for a wheelchair or your knees, a tall table, a low one with soft seats, your back to a wall, out of sight of the door, away from the bar, by the stove, in a patch of light or out of it. Every table can be reached from the door by a way at least 36 inches wide, and the room’s own tool walks the floor to make sure. Sit at a table, order from the bar, and look down to see your table. Where it parts from the books, and says so: a ramp beside the steps, as wide as they are; the ceiling still low, but the fans up between the beams; and your order fetched from the bar or brought to you, whichever you say, and nobody asks why. The measurements are the 2010 ADA Standards’, read on the Access Board’s page. Every pint comes alcohol-free first, in the same glass, at the same size, so nobody can tell from across the room which one anybody has. Ale at cellar temperature, never cold; lemonade with lemonade ice; a mushroom sandwich first and a steak sandwich after it, from the stove. Nothing has a price, and nobody has to order anything to sit down, which is our own Third Places page’s line. Butcher’s words are quoted, not retold: short passages, each naming its book and pages, held to a cap. McAnally’s, Mac and the Dresden Files are his; no wizard drinks here, and nothing is drawn from the fan wiki. Set in Amarante and Brygada 1918, read off their own records. Two shared tools changed for it. table.js can now say how an order reached you, which only this room uses. Big Steep Fermentables’ list of words that press somebody to drink refused the pub’s round tables on its first run, so “round” there now means the round somebody buys. love.css: section 100 is the pub; small screens and print are 101 and 102.

item.title: Four lots where the buildings stop: the Run, the Truck Stop, the Green and the Pile
item.description: Open ground at the far end of the street, at Ryan’s ask: four outdoor lots side by side behind a fence, with a gate into each from the front page, and each lot’s gate through to the next. None of them is a building, so none of them is a shopfront, for the reason the Garden’s gate is not one. On the Map they lie flat down one side of the road, next door to each other. The Run is a dog park with a covered porch of swings, rocking chairs and plush beds, a row of trees and a field for fetch, painted in the colours a dog can see: blues, yellows and greys, and nothing red or green, which the room’s tool checks colour by colour. The ball is blue. Every dog from Rescue A Dog comes out here, put where their mood takes them: press one to meet them, throw the ball, shake the treat tin, or ask one to come and lie by your chair. Dogs who want to be left alone are never asked. Television made for dogs is on the dog telly, one channel of it live. The cats at Pekoe and Purrs and the dogs on the Run now share one script, roam.js, which reads a shelter’s list and puts each animal on a perch by its mood; each room keeps its own words. Checked in the browser: the café works as it did, lap and all. A list of names in what the toys did no longer capitalises a name in the middle of a sentence. Truckin’ Food Court, which everybody calls the Truck Stop: tacos, bánh mì, ramen, treats for dogs and a cooler of cold drinks, each truck doing one thing several ways and leading with a vegan way of doing it, and nothing with a price on it. Every item says what is in it and its allergens, and every drink its caffeine. The oral rehydration solution is the World Health Organization’s recipe to the gram, and every dog treat is checked against the ASPCA’s list of foods to keep from pets. The light comes through the trucks’ striped awnings. The kitchens’ shared allergen engine learned two words: a baguette is wheat bread, which three bánh mì would otherwise have been told had no gluten, and oat flour is oats, not wheat. The Green is a wooded green with a pond, just after the rain: nothing casts a shadow, and everything wet holds the sky along its top edge. An accessible boardwalk goes round the pond, built to the Access Board’s standard for trails, with a trailhead sign giving every figure that standard asks for. You can walk it stop by stop, with beds of herbs, flowers, ferns and vegetables anybody may pick. The Pile is a junk playground of pallets, plywood, rope, an old piano, an old slide and the rest of Ryan’s list, with a den roofed in bubble wrap. Take anything off it and say what it is now, paint it, knock it down. With where junk playgrounds come from, read on the pages named, and our own Play Is Learning. All of Ryan’s films were asked of their own watch pages first. Every one plays. NHK’s RAMEN JAPAN is a door to YouTube, because its channel has switched off showing it on other sites. Set in eight faces, each read off its own record: Lilita One and Mukta, Sansita and Familjen Grotesk, Della Respira and Alegreya, Rubik Wet Paint and Shantell Sans. love.css: sections 96 to 99 are the four lots; small screens and print are 100 and 101.

item.title: Screen a video at Looming Rocks and the Rebellion Rave Room
item.description: A moderator’s Screen a video now works on Looming Rocks’ stage and on the Rebellion Rave Room’s big screen, as it does on the Hermitage’s television. It plays for the moderator who pressed it, and the desk goes back to the bill or the channel list. Catch up and Follow beside them put it on your stage or screen and leave it dark, on the panel every act or channel uses, saying who is hosting it and how long it runs; nothing plays until you press play. At Looming Rocks a video that is on the bill puts that act on the desk. At the rave it is always cued on its own, so it can start where the host is, and it says it may flash. The warning above the rave’s big screen now says a video a moderator puts up from the CB may flash too. Nothing here touches the rig, which still starts only when you ask it to.

item.title: Screen a video on the Hermitage’s television
item.description: A moderator’s Screen a video works on the Solarpunk Hermitage’s campfire television now, as it does on a rack’s screen. It plays on the set at once for the moderator who pressed it, and the remote tunes back to the listing. Catch up and Follow beside them tune it on your set and leave the set off, on the same panel every channel uses, saying who is hosting it and how long it runs; nothing plays until you press play, which is the set’s rule. If the video is one of the listing’s own channels, that channel is what gets tuned.

item.title: Screen a video, from the CB
item.description: Moderators can screen a video in a room without building it into a rack first. Screen a video on the radio takes the address of one YouTube video and puts it up on the first screen of the page you are on, in place of what the screen had, the way a card’s second press does; the button under the screen puts back what was there. It plays on your page and is sent nowhere. It shows only to moderators, and only on pages with a screen. Host it, and the room can follow. Press Host this film once it plays. Anybody who presses Catch up or Follow beside you gets that video’s play button on their own first screen, never the film itself: it says how long the video runs and who put it up, and nothing reaches YouTube until they press it. Only a moderator’s hosting does this, and the server says whose hosting is a moderator’s, so nobody else can put a video on somebody’s screen. Following a host’s link from another room gets it ready too. A host’s beacon now says how long the film runs, so that play button can say it before the press. The privacy page and the CB guide say all of this. Fixed: following a spot’s room link did nothing on most pages, because the page looked for the spot before the radio was there. It looks once the radio is there now.

item.title: Brew and Stew, a woodland tea room
item.description: A new pitch on the Campgrounds: Brew and Stew, pitch 04, a tea room in a cabin at the edge of the trees, and nobody lit it. The light grows in the wood: a pale glow in the joints between the logs, in the moss on the sill and in the little mushrooms at the foot of the walls. The stove is shut iron, giving the room its warmth and none of its light; there is no flame in it anywhere, and nothing in it moves, at any setting. The board: herbal teas, soups and stews, and breads, and everything on it is vegan. Every card says what is in it and its allergens, worked out by Hey, Good Cookin’s engine; every tea is a tisane with no caffeine, worked out by Pekoe and Purrs’ engine; there is no honey, so every tea comes with maple syrup on the side. Nothing on the board is a remedy, and nothing in the room was picked in the wood. Flowers, grasses and twigs on the shelf by the door, each in something to stand in, to take to your table: lavender and oat grass in a jug, birch twigs and catkins in a jar, honesty and willow in a bottle, and more. Every one was grown in the cottage garden or dried from last year’s. Look down at your table, a slice of log with its rings, to see what you asked for. This is the same behaviour as Pekoe and Purrs’ table, moved into one file, table.js, that both rooms use in their own clothes; the café works exactly as it did. The looking-glass by the window, with nothing in it until you put a film up, and a rack of other people’s woodland tea rooms and cottages that Ryan picked. Every one plays here and says how long it runs before you press it. One is held off the rack for now: it has the same title, word for word, as another video on the rack, runs one second longer, and went up two years later on a different channel. On the Campgrounds’ board the tea room’s sign is a cabin with its window dark and its light in its own logs, the fourth kind of light on that board. Set in Macondo, by John Vargas Beltrán, and Livvic, by LV= and Jacques Le Bailly, both under the SIL Open Font License. A job marker (a wooden spoon), a share card, a fractal, the map, Now Playing and the liner notes. In the stylesheet the tea room is section 95, and Small screens and Print are now 96 and 97.

item.title: Pekoe and Purrs, a cat café
item.description: A new shopfront on the street: Pekoe and Purrs, a cat café with a window at every height, each cut to the size of a cat. Coffee, tea and tea sandwiches, and every cat from Rescue A Cat, waiting for a home. The café keeps no list of its own: it reads the shelter’s every time it opens, so a cat adopted this morning has already gone home and one brought in an hour ago is already finding somewhere to sit. Press a cat to meet them: their name and the shelter’s own words about them, and a link straight to that cat’s card at the shelter, where anybody signed on to the CB can adopt them. Pick a cat up and put them on your lap, and look down to see your lap, the cat asleep on it, and your table with whatever you asked for from the menu. A cat the shelter says wants to be left alone is never picked up: there is no button for it. Where a cat goes is its mood’s business, the mood the shelter wrote down when it came in, and never its markings: a cat with three legs gets to the top of the tree like anybody else. At MAX GLITTER the cats wander about by themselves; at Gentle and Regular they stay put until you wave the feather wand, roll the crinkle ball or put down a box. The menu: coffee, not coffee, tea and tea sandwiches, with plenty that is vegan and vegetarian. Every item says what is in it, whether it is vegan, vegetarian or which animal, and its allergens, worked out by the same engine as Hey, Good Cookin’; every drink says how much caffeine, worked out from what is in it. The house milk is oat, the house tea is orange pekoe, which is a grade of black tea and not a flavour, and every cup, mug and pot is the same teal mug. Rescue A Cat: every cat in the shelter now has an address of its own on the page, so a link from the café lands on that cat’s card. The cats themselves are drawn by the same file as always, which can now draw one in daylight and one curled up asleep on a lap. Set in Cherry Bomb One, by Satsuyako, and Gabarito, by Naipe Foundry, both under the SIL Open Font License. A job marker (a felt mouse), a share card, a fractal, the map and the liner notes. In the stylesheet the café is section 94, and Small screens and Print are now 95 and 96.

item.title: Three small things the CB guide turned up
item.description: Move answers when you press it. On the radio and on a call’s window, pressing Move without dragging used to do nothing you could see: the arrow keys were only described to a screen reader, and a click did not even put the keyboard on it. Now a press puts the keyboard on Move, so the arrow keys work straight away, and says in a line how moving works. Dragging is unchanged. The button is called Forget me, and Privacy, the shelters, the job about it at the Adventurer’s Guild and the README now call it that rather than Forget Me. The same job also lost a doubled word: Profile is on your CB radio, not your CB radio radio. A note in the code still said the Faery Yurt had no guest bar. Helen said yes on 2026-09-30, and the note says so now. Nothing a visitor sees changed.

item.title: The CB guide
item.description: A guide to the CB, the street’s radio, part by part and top to bottom, with every button named the way the radio names it: the guest bar and signing on, the bar and its sizes, World and this room, Be seen here, reading and writing messages, reactions, Markdown, pictures, the row of tools, the teleporter, watching films together, calls, Profile and pets, and what moderators see. It ends with every key in one table and a short account of what the radio sends and keeps. It is linked from How the radio works at the Community Center, from the foot of the radio beside the house norms, and from the guest bar for anybody not signed on yet. The Community Center still said links on the channel were only rooms on the street, which stopped being true on 2026-09-29. It now says what its own house norms already did: a link’s words are always its address.

item.title: Architecture
item.description: A new page describing how the site runs, beside How this site is made: that page is the why and this one is the how. It covers the deploy from a push to main, the stylesheet and scripts, the data files and the generators that write parts of pages from them, every checker and what it refuses, the CB’s server side and what it keeps for how long, the morning timers, and every outside service with when it is contacted. Secrets are named and never shown. Its map of what talks to what is boxes and words rather than a picture, so it reflows on a phone and reads aloud in the order a change travels. It is paperwork rather than a room, so it is pinned to the edge of the map with the others, carries no job marker, and takes the plain pages’ quiet clothes.

item.title: The security policy catches up with the CB
item.description: SECURITY.md described the CB as it was on its first day: a handful of functions, one blob and no accounts. It now says what is there: claimed usernames with their own passwords and recovery codes, moderator roles, the private rooms in the Town Hall, pictures on the channel, the Brass Tacks Board and its feed, and 8x8’s calls and webhooks. The list of what is worth reporting grew with it, and so did the list of secrets kept in Netlify’s environment, by name only.

item.title: Hey, Good Cookin’
item.description: A community kitchen on the street, at Ryan’s ask and in his words: come if you’re hungry for food or for knowledge, no one is turned away, you don’t have to pay and you don’t have to volunteer. Cafeteria-style self-service, sit-down seating, and a communication badge placard on every table: green for open seating, yellow for ask if you know somebody, red for please don’t sit here, each with its shape and its word so colour is never the only sign. It is a hall on a cold day with every pot on, its windows steamed up, and the only sharp light in it is where a drop has run down the glass. An omnivorous menu with plenty of vegan and vegetarian: a hot line for every day of the week, posted whole, with the vegan pan first every day, and stations from the soup kettles to the plain things that never change. Every dish card says what is in it, whether it is vegan or vegetarian or which animal it came from, and which of the FDA’s nine major allergens it has, and gluten, worked out from the ingredients so the two lines cannot disagree. No calorie counts, and nothing about what a dish does for you. The line and every table are built to work from a wheelchair, to the 2010 ADA Standards’ numbers, each linked to its section; the standard asks for one seat in twenty and here it is every seat. Help is offered and never assumed, and anybody who cannot do the line today can sit down and have the board and the plate brought. Cooking classes written in full, each saying how long it takes, what it sounds and smells like, and that it can all be done sitting down, with FoodSafety.gov’s temperatures beside anything that needs them. No sign-up, no register, no grades. A rack of the last month from cooking channels Ryan chose, videos and shorts, which plays where it hangs or on the teaching screen, and refills itself every morning on the same timer as the other racks. The room says plainly that nobody here watched the videos first. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press. Set in Corben, by Vernon Adams, and Parkinsans, by Red Stone, both new to the street. A job marker is on the floor, and every source is in the liner notes.

item.title: Learning Large
item.description: A new shopfront about learning, making and knowledge gardening with generative AI, at Ryan’s ask, with his tagline over the door: Models are spiky. Humans are too. Learning, making, and knowledge gardening, together. It is a glasshouse at night under the old red and blue grow lamps, and nothing in it is green, because under that light a leaf has no green to give back. The argument is our own AI pages’, starting from AI at Stimpunks: spiky profiles, a model’s peaks and troughs as our pages describe them, competency networks and the legibility test, harm reduction and knowing how the tools work, making rather than being made into data, and a garden that belongs to the people who tend it. Every quotation is checked word for word against our page on every build, and says where it was read. The sowing log is this street as a worked example: times something came up wrong here, most of them Claude’s, and who or what noticed, each linked to the day it was written up below. A rack of the latest month from AI channels Ryan chose, videos and shorts, which plays where it hangs or on the screen on the potting bench, and refills itself every morning on the same timer as The Open Notebook’s log. The room says plainly that Ryan chose the channels and nobody here watched the videos first. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press, and there is no chat box in the room: nothing you do here is sent to an AI. Set in Recursive, by Arrow Type and Stephen Nixon, in its casual cut, and Fira Sans, by Carrois Apostrophe for Mozilla, both new to the street. A job marker is on the floor, and the credits are in the liner notes.

item.title: Two more channels in The Open Notebook
item.description: The monthly log has two more channels, at Ryan’s ask: Lori Ann Tata and Mark Your Pages, at the end of his list. Their last month of videos and shorts is in it now, and it refills with the rest every morning. Both are credited in the liner notes.

item.title: The Open Notebook
item.description: A new shopfront for journaling, at Ryan’s ask, and he chose its name: a desk under a window with a notebook lying open on it since first light, so every hour’s sun is on the page at once, each with its time written under it. It leads with Ryan’s own piece in full, on keeping a bullet journal, a junk journal and an interstitial journal in the same notebook, which he gave to the street under its licence. Its lists of videos have been moved to the collection further down, and a line in the margin of the piece says so wherever that happened. The questions from the Infodumplings where he shared it follow it, word for word from our write-up of that evening, Star Stuff and L★S included. There is nowhere on the page to answer them, on purpose: they are for your own paper. A laptop beside the notebook, and two racks that can go up on it: the collection, every video the piece points at, on a shelf for each practice; and the monthly log, the last month of videos and shorts from journaling, stationery and notebook channels Ryan chose. The log refills itself every morning on the same timer as the kitchen’s telly, and the room says plainly that Ryan chose the channels and nobody here watched the videos first. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press, and every video says how long it runs before you do. Set in Doto, by Óliver Lalan, whose letters are made of round dots like the page, and Rosario, by Omnibus-Type, both new to the street. A job marker is on the floor, and the credits are in the liner notes.

item.title: More comics at Laughingstock, and The Daily Tism on the bar
item.description: Laughingstock’s bill has new comics on it, at Ryan’s ask: Joe Wells, Fern Brady, Tim Renkow, Stuart Laws, Pierre Novellie, Hannah Gadsby, Lara Ricote and Rosie Jones, plus the AJ Wilkerson specials that had gone onto our playlist since the bill was last read. Every set says how long it runs before you press it, and every one was checked that day to see that it plays and can be shown here. Tim Renkow’s sets say they are very dark humour before you press them. The bill works like the racks in the newer rooms now. Every set plays where it hangs or goes up on the stage in place of the whole night, and taking it off puts the whole night back without starting it. The bill folds away. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press. Stuart Laws’ two sets are on the bill and not on the playlist yet, so putting the whole night on does not reach them, and the room says so under the bill. A Fern Brady clip from The Last Leg is not on the bill at all: it does not play outside the UK. Fern Brady’s full special is on the bill. The Daily Tism is on the bar: a satirical news site about being Autistic, and its audio sitcom, It’s a Superpower?? Not stand-up, and in the room anyway. Both are links; nothing of theirs plays here. Freak Accident’s note no longer calls it the longest set on the bill, which stopped being true the day Rosie Jones’ special went on. The room’s tool now refuses a note that says longest, shortest or newest. Credits are in the liner notes.

item.title: A telly in the kitchen
item.description: Vital Plant Living has a telly, at Ryan’s ask: plant-based cooks on YouTube, in the order he listed them, with the last month of what each one has put up, videos and shorts both, newest first under each cook. Each one plays where it hangs or goes up on the telly, a short upright, and says how long it runs before you press it. Nothing loads from YouTube until you do. It refills itself every morning, on the same timer as The Feed and The Doom Scoop, and anything older than a month goes off the end. The room says when it was last filled, and says plainly that Ryan chose the cooks and nobody here watched the videos first. Every title is the cook’s own, as written. The cooks are credited in the liner notes.

item.title: Search every word on the street
item.description: The search box on the street and on the Map searches every page now, not only the rooms’ names, as all our other sites already do. Rooms found by name still come first. Under them come the sections of pages that hold every word you typed, each linked to the section rather than the top of the page, with a few lines round the first match, and the changelog after everything else. A quotation is never cut down in a result. A match inside a quotation shows who it is credited to and where it is, and not a trimmed piece of somebody else’s words. A snippet that would start or end inside a quotation in our own sentences is widened to hold all of it. It reads every page’s own words, written into search-index.json by a new tool each time the site is checked. It leaves out the parts the morning timers refill (the Doom Scoop’s cabinet, The Feed’s board, the kitchen telly and the Now Playing bill), the job markers, and the lyric printed in full at The Small Hours, which is there with permission and not under this site’s licence. Why not Pagefind, which one of our sites uses: it runs WebAssembly, which would loosen the part of this site’s security policy that decides what scripts may run; its index is a folder of many small files that would change in every morning’s commit; and both of the machines that publish here would need it installed. A file of our own words, searched in your browser, is how most of our sites do it. The file is fetched from this site the first time you type, and what you type never leaves your browser. The privacy page says so.

item.title: “Music” finds the music rooms
item.description: Searching for “music” found nothing, because none of the music rooms’ own descriptions used the word: they said songs, records and concerts. Each of those descriptions says music now, in a few words and nothing else changed: Pink Pony Club, The Chappell, Club Chronic, The Den, Black Leather Lagoon, Looming Rocks, The Live Room, Dance, Punks, The Small Hours, the Rebellion Rave Room and Now Playing. The share cards are drawn from a different line and have not changed.

item.title: Finding a room by what it is about
item.description: A search box near the top of the street and of the Map, for Helen Edgar, who asked for a search bar at the top. It is on those two pages and nowhere else, Ryan’s call, because the teleporter already searches from every page and a bar across the top of every room would lay the street’s furniture over all of them. What it finds are ordinary links, and Enter goes to the first. Typing “fire” in the teleporter finds The Campfire now, as Helen Edgar asked. It looks inside the words of a room’s name as well as at their starts, so a part of a word is enough. It also searches each room’s own description, the summary at the top of its page, so a keyword finds the rooms it is about. A room found that way shows the words it was found in. Rooms found by their name come first, then rooms found by their description, each group in walking order. Every word you type has to be found, and a plural also finds the singular. The box, the radio and the guest bar all search this way, and a new check makes sure they never find different rooms. Nothing about a search is sent anywhere.

item.title: Share cards that stay put between two Macs
item.description: The share cards stopped trading places between Ryan’s Mac and Helen Edgar’s.
